title: Long-Sightedness (Hypermetropia)
short_intro: Long-sightedness, or hypermetropia, is a defect of vision where distant objects are seen clearly but near objects appear blurred because light rays focus behind the retina. It is corrected by using a converging (convex) lens of appropriate focal length.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of hypermetropia, identification of the defect, near point shift from normal (25 cm) to a greater distance (D'), and calculation of power and focal length of the correcting convex lens.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed analysis of retinal image formation, crystalline lens accommodation limits, shift in the least distance of distinct vision, and calculations involving combined optical systems (eye plus corrective lens) situated at a given corneal distance.

prerequisites: Geometrical optics and refraction through spherical surfaces
Lens maker's formula and thin lens formula
Anatomy of the human eye and accommodation

concept_notes.heading: Anatomical and Physiological Causes of Hypermetropia
bullets: The eyeball is unusually short along its optical axis, causing the retina to lie closer to the cornea-lens system than the focal point of the relaxed eye.
The curvature of the cornea or the crystalline lens is insufficient, leading to a weaker converging power than required for normal vision.
The near point of the eye shifts away from the standard reference distance of 25 cm to a greater distance D', so that rays from an object at 25 cm form a virtual image beyond the retina.

concept_notes.heading: Optical Correction Mechanism
bullets: A converging lens (convex lens) is placed in front of the eye to supplement the optical power of the defective eye.
The corrective lens forms a virtual image of an object placed at the normal near point (u = -25 cm) at the patient's actual shifted near point (v = -D').
The net focal length of the combined spectacle lens and eye system allows parallel or diverging rays from near objects to converge precisely on the retina.

concept_notes.heading: Power Sign Convention and Dioptric Strength
bullets: The focal length (f) and power (P) of the corrective convex lens are always positive.
Power is measured in diopters (D) when the focal length is expressed in meters.
If a spectacle lens is worn at a specific distance (d) from the cornea, this gap must be accounted for in precise clinical and optical calculations.

concept_notes.heading: Comparison with Presbyopia and Myopia
bullets: Unlike myopia (near-sightedness) where the image falls in front of the retina and is corrected by concave lenses, hypermetropia focuses behind the retina and requires convex lenses.
Presbyopia involves a similar need for convex lenses due to age-related loss of accommodation, but hypermetropia is fundamentally a structural refractive error independent of age.
Astigmatism involves non-spherical curvatures, whereas hypermetropia is spherically symmetrical.

derivations.title: Derivation of Corrective Lens Formula
derivations.conditions: An eye with hypermetropia has a near point at D' instead of the normal near point D (25 cm). The spectacle lens is placed in contact with the eye (negligible corneal distance).
steps: Substitute the object distance u equal to the normal near point with sign convention: u = -D = -25 \text{ cm}.
Substitute the image distance v equal to the patient's actual near point with sign convention: v = -D'.

derivations.title: Derivation with Corneal Distance Consideration
derivations.conditions: The corrective spectacle lens is placed at a distance d from the cornea of the hypermetropic eye.
steps: The object is placed at the normal near point distance D from the lens, so u = -D.
The lens must form a virtual image at a position such that the eye can view it clearly. The eye's actual near point is at distance D' from the cornea.
Therefore, the image distance from the corrective lens must be v = -(D' - d).
Apply the thin lens formula: \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-(D' - d)} - \frac{1}{-D}

graphs_and_experiments.title: Ray Diagram of Uncorrected Hypermetropic Eye
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An eyeball showing parallel or diverging rays from a near object (at 25 cm) intersecting behind the retina.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that the eye's converging power is inadequate, causing the focal point to lie behind the retina.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Often asked in TGT/PGT descriptive questions to test identification of the defect and ray tracing.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Ray Diagram of Corrected Hypermetropic Eye
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A convex lens placed before the eye refracting incoming rays from a near object (25 cm) such that they appear to emanate from the shifted near point D' and converge precisely on the retina.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows how the convex lens converges the light beforehand, reducing the required convergence burden on the eye's crystalline lens.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Evaluates understanding of virtual object-image relationships in corrective optics.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Power vs Near Point Recession Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve plotting required corrective lens power (P in diopters) on the y-axis against the shifted near point distance (D' in cm) on the x-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: As the near point recedes further away from the eye (larger D'), a stronger positive power lens is required to achieve correction.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in numerical-based conceptual MCQs where trend analysis is required.

solved_numericals.question: A hypermetropic person has a near point of 50 cm. Calculate the focal length and power of the convex lens required to enable him to read a book held at 25 cm.
solution_steps: Identify given values: Normal near point u = -25 cm, Defective near point v = -50 cm.
Calculate focal length: f = +50 \text{ cm} = +0.5 \text{ m}.
solved_numericals.answer: Focal length = +50 cm (+0.5 m), Power = +2.0 D

solved_numericals.question: The near point of a hypermetropic eye is 1.0 m. What is the power of the corrective lens required if the spectacles are worn 2.0 cm in front of the cornea? Assume standard near point to be 25 cm.
solution_steps: Identify standard near point D = 25 cm = 0.25 m, so u = -0.25 m.
Identify patient's actual near point from cornea D' = 1.0 m = 100 cm.
Image distance from the lens v = -(D' - d) = -(100 - 2) \text{ cm} = -98 \text{ cm} = -0.98 \text{ m}.

solved_numericals.question: A person cannot see objects distinctly placed closer than 75 cm. What should be the power of the lens in spectacles if he wishes to read a newspaper at 25 cm?
solution_steps: Object distance u = -25 cm, Image distance v = -75 cm.
Convert focal length to meters: f = \frac{75}{2} \text{ cm} = 37.5 \text{ cm} = 0.375 \text{ m}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: The eye is treated as a centered optical system with a single equivalent refracting surface and thin lens approximation holds for the corrective eyewear.

Limitation: Physiological variations in accommodation, pupil size diffraction effects, and off-axis aberrations (astigmatism of oblique incidence) in spectacle lenses are neglected in elementary calculations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Long-sighted people cannot see distant objects clearly.
common_misconceptions.correct: Long-sighted people can see distant objects clearly; they have difficulty seeing near objects.
common_misconceptions.why: The term 'long-sighted' refers to the eye being able to focus on distant objects well, while the near point has receded.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Concave lenses are used to correct hypermetropia.
common_misconceptions.correct: Convex lenses are used to correct hypermetropia.
common_misconceptions.why: Hypermetropia requires converging power to shift the focal point forward onto the retina, which is achieved using convex lenses.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The near point of a hypermetropic eye is closer than 25 cm.
common_misconceptions.correct: The near point of a hypermetropic eye is further than 25 cm (e.g., 50 cm or 1 m).
common_misconceptions.why: A closer near point is characteristic of myopia, whereas hypermetropia causes the near point to recede.

quick_revision: Hypermetropia is corrected using a positive (convex) lens of appropriate focal length.
The near point in hypermetropia shifts farther away than the standard 25 cm.
Image formation in an uncorrected hypermetropic eye occurs behind the retina.
